rosedale_wife.text: Welcome to Rosedale. The dale was not always this quiet. In the 1800s it was full of ironstone mines.
A railway carried the ore over the moor, and the old stone kilns still stand as a reminder.
Down at the beck you might see a dipling bobbing on a stone, then walking straight under the water. We never tire of it.
Our Joe says it is mardy weather, which means grumpy, when it drizzles all day. He says it a lot. He is a mardy lad.

then.text: They went back to their own bit of hill without being told. I stood at the gate like a daft lad. Dale's lot, my lot, same flock now.
I lent Hannah the dog for lambing. Dale will not hear a word against his girl, and he is right.
Dale has gone green, I told him. He said I was welcome to a clipboard. We are still speaking.
Whatever Dale decides, I will abide by it. And I will not say a word out of turn at the mart.
Tell him what I said, and tell him I would sooner be turned down by Dale than praised by anyone else.

else.text: You will be the one Dale has sent. He is a proud man and a good farmer, and he would hate me for saying it, but his is the best flock on this moor.
I would take the tenancy and the ewes together, keep them on their own hill and put my shepherd in the house. It would double my acreage in a year when prices are telling everyone to shrink.
I will be straight about it: it is good for me. It is also the only way that flock stays a flock. Split it or sell it, and those are just ewes.
What I cannot give is Hannah's choice. If she wants it, it is hers by every right but the paperwork, and I would not stand in her way.
Morning. Rosedale used to have ironstone kilns smoking all down the dale. Now it has me and a very loud dog.
